Thanks Arjun — good summary and the sketch helps. Short version up front: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) + tight egress allowlists on your perimeter is the cleanest compliance posture for AuroraMed; fallback path is S2S VPN with egress NAT + proxy for legacy on-prem systems that cannot reach endpoints. VPC peering is simplest for very low latency but is the worst from a least-privilege standpoint because it expands your attack surface across subnets.

High-level tradeoffs: 
- PrivateLink (recommended): keeps control plane and inference endpoints reachable via interface endpoints; you control DNS + security groups so only the relevant hosts can talk to Redwood. Auditable and fits compliance requests to restrict outbound targets. Slightly more operational work (endpoint setup, SGs, endpoint policies) but significantly better isolation.
- S2S VPN + NAT/Proxy: good when on-prem systems cannot use endpoint DNS or IPs. Allows you to centralize egress through a proxy (we can integrate with your secure web proxy) for traffic inspection. Slightly higher latency and requires HA VPN + clear NAT rules.
- VPC Peering: very low latency and native cross-VPC traffic; however, it effectively extends your VPC into ours and requires careful routing restrictions. Not recommended if your compliance team requires strict outbound scoping.

I've sketched an action checklist and a minimal policy template and attached them. Quick asks for us: what latency window is acceptable for inference calls from your on-prem clients (p50/p95), and do you have an existing secure proxy we want to force traffic through?

I'll be brief on an operational checklist in a follow-up message — want to make sure it maps to your procurement timeline.

—Markus Klein
Director, Infrastructure Solutions, Redwood Inference

Arjun / team — thanks for the clarity on latency and proxy. Based on AuroraMed's constraints and the preference for strict outbound scoping, our recommended path: 

1) Primary: PrivateLink interface endpoints for Redwood control plane + model endpoints. Configure endpoint policies to only permit the Aurora VPC subnets used by the inference gateway. Use AWS Private DNS (alias records) to resolve service hostnames to the endpoint IPs inside the VPC. Enforce mTLS for service-to-service traffic; where mTLS cannot be adopted immediately, require TLS and lock down SGs/IPs.

2) On-prem access: S2S VPN (HA pair) that terminates to a NAT + BlueCoat proxy cluster on Aurora side. Force on-prem clients to egress through the proxy so Security can inspect requests. We will provide a minimal set of destination IPs/hostnames that must be allowlisted on the proxy (we'll send this as a separate CSV).

3) Avoid VPC peering for now: recommend against peering unless you need sub-10ms median and are willing to extend routing controls and cross-account flow logs. If you later choose peering for a high-throughput, low-latency use case, use route table tags, explicit prefix-lists, and a narrow set of subnet-level ACLs.

Operational checklist (high level):
- Provision PrivateLink endpoints + endpoint policies (2–3 business days after approvals)
- Configure DNS alias records and internal certs (1–2 business days with certs ready)
- Stand up HA VPN pair and NAT + proxy rules for on-prem (3–5 business days with network team)
- Update observability hooks and access logs to forward to Aurora's SIEM (we'll share our log schema)
- DocuSign SOW + procurement: we attached a SOW snippet and cost estimates for endpoint hours/data.

Next steps: Kimberly will draft the SOW snippet and cost line-items; Irene, can you share the proxy ACL template and cert contact? Arjun, if procurement needs a one-pager, we can produce that today.

I'll also attach the allowlist CSV once we finalize the endpoints.

—Markus
Director, Infrastructure Solutions, Redwood Inference
